messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Bank Teller
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Elena, a fifty-five-year-old bank teller, was a child when her family fled the civil wars in Central America. She had been twelve, walking with her older brother and her mother along a dirt road, when a mortar round landed fifty yards ahead of them. The sound was not a bang but a percussive slam that seemed to push the air out of her lungs. She remembered the wet, gritty feel of the mud and ash that sprayed across her face and arms as she hit the ground—a texture that, even now, forty-three years later, would make her stomach clench if she accidentally touched something similar, like the damp grout in the staff break room at the bank. Her brother had been thrown to the other side of the road. He did not get up. She had tried to crawl toward him, but her mother’s hand was gripping her wrist, pulling her into the ditch. She never saw him alive again. When she tried to tell this story—to her ex-husband, to a therapist she saw once, to herself—she would start with the walk, then the sound, then the texture, but she could never get the sequence straight. She would lose the thread, and the whole thing would feel like a movie she had watched rather than a thing that had actually happened to her. It was so extreme, so absurd, that some part of her still could not believe it was her life.

The aftermath settled into her body before it settled into her mind. For months after the bombing, she could not tolerate the feel of damp cloth, or wet leaves, or the condensation on a cold soda can. She learned to avoid those textures without thinking. But the more lasting change was how she learned to move through the world. By the time she arrived in the United States at fifteen, she had become a person who never stopped scanning. In any room, she knew where the exits were. She watched people’s hands. She studied faces and body language the way other people studied menus—automatically, constantly, looking for the flicker of intention that might mean danger. She had come to believe, with a certainty that felt like common sense, that the world was a dangerous place and that she had to be on guard all the time. Nothing in her life felt meaningful anymore; the things other people cared about—retirement plans, holiday parties, grandchildren—seemed like decorations on a sinking ship.

At work, she was efficient and quiet. Her job as a teller required her to be pleasant and to handle cash, but it also required her to sit with her back to the open lobby, which she hated. She had learned to angle her chair so she could see the door in her peripheral vision. When customers talked about losing loved ones—a parent, a spouse, a pet—she felt a physical reaction: her heart would pound, her palms would sweat, and she would have to excuse herself to the break room. She could not explain why those conversations hit her so hard. She just knew she had to get away. Her colleagues thought she was cold or shy. They did not know that she was fighting the urge to run every time someone said the word lost.

The worst moments were the bangs. A car backfiring in the parking lot. A dropped metal tray in the kitchen. A balloon popping at a child’s birthday party. Each time, her body would lurch before her mind could catch up. Her heart would hammer, her muscles would lock, and she would be back on that road for a split second—not in memory, but in sensation. She had learned to brace for these moments, to scan the environment for any sign of a loud noise, but she could not avoid them entirely. They came without warning.

She had been divorced for fifteen years. Her ex-husband had told her she was impossible to live with, that she was always looking at him like he was a stranger. She had not disagreed. She had not been able to explain that she was looking at everyone that way. She lived alone now, in a small apartment with neutral-colored walls. She kept the television volume low. She did not invite people over. She had come to believe that this was simply what her life was now: a long, quiet watch.

What finally brought her to seek help was not a crisis, but a slow recognition that she was tired. Tired of the scanning, tired of the startle, tired of the way her own history felt like someone else’s story. She had walked into a community clinic and filled out a questionnaire. The therapist asked her what she hoped for. Elena said she did not know. But what she was most afraid of, she admitted quietly, was that she would spend the rest of her life in that ditch, feeling the grit on her skin, and never find a way back to the road.
